source_text: Proinde fatendum est nescire quidem mortuos quid hic agatur, sed dum hic agitur, postea uero audire ab eis. qui hinc ad eos moriendo pergunt, non quidem omnia, sed quae sinuntur indicare, qui sinuntur etiam ista meminisse, et quae illos, quibus haec indicant, oportet audire.. possunt et ab , angelis, qui rebus, quae aguntur hic, praesto sunt, audire aliquid mortui, quod unumquemque illorum audire debere iudicat, cui cuncta subiecta sunt. nisi enim essent angeli, qui possent interesse et uiuorum et mortuorum locis, non dixisset dominus Iesus: contigit autem mori inopem illum et auferri ab angelis in sinum Abrahae. nunc ergo hic, nunc ibi esse potuerunt, qui hinc illuc quem deus uoluit abstulerunt. possunt etiam spiritus mortuorum aliqua, quae hic aguntur, quae necessarium est eos nosse et quos necessarium est ea nosse, non solum praesentia uel praeterita, uerum etiam futura spiritu dei reuelante cognoscere, sicut non omnes homines, sed prophetae, dum hic uiuerent, cognoscebant, nec ipsi omnia, sed quae illis esse reuelanda dei prouidentia iudicabat. mitti quoque ad uiuos aliquos ex mortuis, sicut e contrario Paulus ex uiuis in paradisum raptus est, diuina scriptura testatur. nam Samuhel propheta defunctus uiuo regi Sauli etiam futura praedixit: quamuis nonnulli non ipsum fuisse, qui potuisset magicis artibus euocari, sed aliquem spiritum tam malis operibus congruentem illius existiment similitudinem figurasse: cum liber Ecclesiasticus, quem Iesus filius Sirach scripsisse traditur et propter eloquii nonnullam similitudinem Salomonis pronuntiatur, contineat in laude patrum, quod Samuhel etiam mortuus prophetauerit. sed si et huic libro ex Hebraeorum quia in eo non est canone contradicitur, quid de Moyse dicturi sumus, qui certe et in Deuteronomio mortuus et in euangelio cum Helia, qui mortuus non est, legitur adparuisse uiuentibus?
thought_title: The dead can learn of the living afterwards
orientation: Augustine is answering the question how the dead can know what happens among the living, since he has just shown that Abraham learned of the rich man's life only after death.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore it must be admitted that the dead indeed do not know what is done here, but while it is done here, but afterwards they hear it from those who go from here to them by dying, not indeed all things, but what things those are permitted to indicate, who are permitted also to remember these things, and what things it is fitting for those to hear, to whom they indicate these things. The dead can also hear something from angels, who are present at the things which are done here, something which he judges each one of them ought to hear, to whom all things are subject. For unless there were angels, who could be present in the places both of the living and of the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: but it happened that that poor man died and was carried away by angels into the bosom of Abraham. Therefore they were able to be now here, now there, who carried away from here to there the one whom God willed. The spirits of the dead can also know some things which are done here, which it is necessary for them to know and whom it is necessary to know these things, not only present or past things, but also future things, by the spirit of God revealing, just as not all men, but the prophets, while they lived here, knew, and not even they all things, but what things the providence of God judged were to be revealed to them. That some from the dead are also sent to the living, just as on the contrary Paul was caught up from the living into paradise, divine scripture testifies. For Samuel the prophet, dead, predicted even future things to the living king Saul: although some think that it was not he himself, who could have been called forth by magic arts, but that some spirit suited to such evil works figured his likeness: since the book of Ecclesiasticus, which Jesus son of Sirach is handed down to have written and is pronounced to be Solomon's because of some likeness of eloquence, contains in the praise of the fathers, that Samuel even dead prophesied. But if objection is made also to this book from the canon of the Hebrews because it is not in it, what are we to say about Moses, who certainly is read both to have died in Deuteronomy and to have appeared in the gospel with Elijah, who did not die, to the living?

choices.why: The gerundive of obligation with 'est' expresses necessity; 'admitted' captures the concessive force of conceding a point in the argument.
'dum' with the indicative present marks contemporaneous time; 'here' renders 'hic' as the realm of the living, matching the contrast with 'hinc' and 'illuc'.
rejected: as long as it happens here
during the time it is done here

choices.english: what things those are permitted to indicate
choices.why: The passive 'sinuntur' with the infinitive 'indicare' means permission is granted to the subject; the relative clause keeps the restrictive force of 'non omnia, sed'.
rejected: what they are allowed to point out
the things they are suffered to declare

choices.term: nunc ergo hic, nunc ibi esse potuerunt
choices.english: Therefore they were able to be now here, now there
choices.why: 'nunc...nunc' is the correlative pair meaning 'at one time...at another time'; keeping 'now...now' preserves the Latin idiom and the point that angels can be in either place as needed.
rejected: So they could be sometimes here, sometimes there
Therefore they had the power to be both here and there

choices.why: The glossary gives 'spiritus' as 'spirit' for the soul of a deceased person; the genitive plural 'mortuorum' is rendered as 'of the dead' to keep the distinction from living human spirits.
'figurasse' means to shape or form a likeness; 'similitudinem' is the glossary term 'likeness' for an image seen in a vision, not the person himself.

pass_b_english: So it must be admitted that the dead do not know what is done here while it is done here, but afterwards they hear it from those who pass from here to them by dying—not everything, but what those are permitted to indicate, who are also permitted to remember these things, and what those to whom they indicate them ought to hear. The dead can also hear something from the angels, who are present at the things that are done here, whatever the One to whom all things are subject judges that each of them ought to hear. For if there were no angels who could be present in the places of both the living and the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: “It happened that the poor man died and was carried away by the angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22). Therefore they were able to be now here, now there, who carried from here to there whomever God willed—namely, the angels. The spirits of the dead can also know some things that are done here—things that it is necessary for them to know, and for those whom it is necessary to know them—not only present or past things but even future things, by the Spirit of God revealing them, just as not all human beings but the prophets knew them while they lived here, and not even they knew all things, but only what God’s providence judged should be revealed to them. Divine Scripture also testifies that some of the dead are sent to the living, just as, on the other hand, Paul was caught up from the living into paradise. For the prophet Samuel, after his death, foretold even future things to King Saul while he was alive; although some think that it was not Samuel himself—who could have been called up by magic arts—but some spirit suited to such evil works that figured his likeness. Yet the book of Sirach, which Ben Sira is handed down to have written and which is pronounced Solomon’s because of a certain likeness of eloquence, contains in the Praise of the Fathers that Samuel prophesied even after death. But if this book is also contradicted by the Hebrews because it is not in their canon, what are we to say about Moses, who certainly both died in Deuteronomy and is read to have appeared to the living in the Gospel with Elijah, who did not die?

problems.why: lint glossary: use the modern name 'Ben Sira' ('Jesus son of Sirach')

fixed: Replaced 'Jesus son of Sirach' with 'Ben Sira' per the work brief's names glossary.

problems.quote: who carried away from here to there the one whom God willed
problems.source_quote: qui hinc illuc quem deus uoluit abstulerunt
problems.why: The relative clause modifies the angels; 'abstulerunt' = 'carried away', but the English makes 'who carried away' seem to refer back to 'they', creating confusion about whether it's the angels or someone else.
problems.fix: who carried away from here to there whomever God willed

problems.quote: contains in the praise of the fathers
problems.why: 'contineat' is subjunctive in a relative clause of characteristic; 'contains' is fine, but 'in laude patrum' = 'in the Praise of the Fathers', the title of a section of Sirach (ch. 44-50), not just 'in the praise of the fathers'.
problems.fix: contains in the Praise of the Fathers
problems.ruling: 'in laude patrum' refers to Sirach 44-50 'Praise of the Fathers,' a specific section title, not generic praise.

Changed 'in the praise of the fathers' to 'in the Praise of the Fathers' to reflect the section title 'in laude patrum' in Sirach.

problems.quote: But if this book is also contradicted from the canon of the Hebrews because it is not in it
problems.source_quote: sed si et huic libro ex Hebraeorum quia in eo non est canone contradicitur
problems.why: Source means 'if this book is contradicted by the Hebrews because it is not in their canon'; English garbles agency.
problems.fix: But if this book is also contradicted by the Hebrews because it is not in their canon
problems.ruling: Latin 'ex Hebraeorum...canone' = 'from the canon of the Hebrews'; English 'contradicted from' garbles agency, making Hebrews the source of contradiction rather than their canon.

edits.old: But if this book is also contradicted from the canon of the Hebrews because it is not in it
edits.new: But if this book is also contradicted by the Hebrews because it is not in their canon

fixed: Corrected the agency of the contradiction: the source says the book is contradicted by the Hebrews (ex Hebraeorum canone), not contradicted from the canon.

problems.quote: who carried away from here to there whomever God willed
problems.source_quote: qui hinc illuc quem deus uoluit abstulerunt
problems.why: The antecedent of 'qui' is the angels, not a general 'they'. The English 'who carried away' is ambiguous; 'qui' refers back to 'angeli' from the previous clause about angels being present in both places.
problems.fix: who carried from here to there whomever God willed—namely, the angels.

problems.quote: who certainly is read to have died in Deuteronomy
problems.source_quote: qui certe et in Deuteronomio mortuus et in euangelio cum Helia, qui mortuus non est, legitur adparuisse uiuentibus
problems.why: The Latin says Moses 'is read to have appeared' (legitur adparuisse), with 'mortuus' (having died) as a participle parallel to 'adparuisse'. The English 'is read to have died' misreads the syntax: 'mortuus' is not governed by 'legitur' directly but is a participle; Moses is read to have died AND to have appeared.
problems.fix: who certainly both died in Deuteronomy and is read to have appeared to the living in the Gospel with Elijah, who did not die
problems.ruling: 'legitur' governs 'adparuisse' only; 'mortuus' is participle. 'Is read to have died' misreads syntax, conflating two distinct claims.
